2610.28736.title: Saturation Level of the Streaming Instability

figures.caption:
Figure 1.— Confirming the saturation prediction along three axes of variables.
The vertical black dashed lines indicate the anchor case, while the thick gray lines are the theoretical prediction (eq. 7). The scattered points represent various numerical results, slightly offset horizontally for clarity. Open symbols show literature results: JY07 for Johansen and Youdin [19]; BS10 for Bai and Stone [2]; SK18 for Schreiber and Klahr [32]; HB22 for Huang and Bai [17], BYZ24 for Baronett et al. [4].
Filled circles are results from this work: these are run with a box size of $0.1h$, except for those circled with black rings – they have smaller box sizes and thus higher effective resolutions (see Table 1).
Numerical convergence is challenging where grains are small ($St\ll 1$) or dilute ($\epsilon\ll 1$).

2610.28736.abstract: In proto-planetary disks, gas turbulence can cluster dust grains and catalyze the formation of planetesimals. This process depends on the strength of the turbulence. Here, we evaluate the turbulence strength that is induced by the streaming instability. Based on the amount of free energy available, we estimate the viscous parameter to be alpha ~ St Pi^2 f(epsilon), where St (< 1) is the Stokes number of the streaming grains, Pi is the dimensionless pressure gradient, and f (epsilon) is an explicit function of epsilon, the local dust-to-gas density ratio. This estimate explains the results of many previous studies, and is also supported by our additional tailor-made simulations. We discuss two easy applications of our result, one is a self-consistent dust scale height, one is the astrophysical relevance of a pressure bump. Lastly, while this work allows one to characterize the streaming turbulence, we emphasize our current inability to connect the strength of turbulence to the formation of planetesimals.

2610.28755.title: Systematic Uncertainties in Rocky Exoplanet Reflected Light from Incomplete Laboratory BRDF Measurements

figures.caption:
Figure 1: 
Allowed photometric parameter space in the $(b,B_{0})$ plane at fixed laboratory geometry $(i_{0},e_{0},g_{0})=(30^{\circ},0^{\circ},30^{\circ})$. Colors represent the misfit $\log_{10}\chi^{2}$ between the model reflectance and a reference laboratory reflectance $r_{\rm target}$. Instead of a localized solution, the allowed parameter space forms an extended valley, demonstrating that multiple photometric solutions reproduce the same single-geometry laboratory spectrum. The red point marks the reference parameter combination used to define $r_{\rm target}$; it is not a uniquely recovered solution. The white curve marks the analytic locus defined by $r(i_{0},e_{0},g_{0})=r_{\rm target}$, along which multiple photometric solutions reproduce the same single-geometry reflectance.

Figure 2: 
Phase curves corresponding to photometric parameter combinations $(b,B_{0})$ that reproduce the same laboratory reflectance at the reference geometry $(i_{0},e_{0},g_{0})=(30^{\circ},0^{\circ},30^{\circ})$. The parameters are explored over $-0.3\leq b\leq 0.7$ and $0\leq B_{0}\leq 3$, while the single-scattering albedo and opposition-surge width are fixed at $\omega=0.6$ and $h=0.1$, respectively. All solutions intersect at the measured phase angle $g_{0}=30^{\circ}$ by construction, but diverge away from the laboratory geometry, particularly toward small phase angles where opposition effects dominate. This demonstrates that identical laboratory reflectance measurements can correspond to substantially different angular scattering behavior.

Figure 3: 
Propagation of incomplete angular constraints into the inferred single-scattering albedo spectrum for the RELAB spectrum BIR1DD065 of olivine from the Martian meteorite NWA 2737. Top: laboratory reflectance spectrum used as the input constraint. Middle: ensemble of inferred $\omega(\lambda)$ solutions obtained by sampling the angular-scattering parameters $(b,B_{0},h)$ and inverting the Hapke model wavelength-by-wavelength to reproduce the measured reflectance at the laboratory geometry $(i_{0},e_{0},g_{0})=(30^{\circ},0^{\circ},30^{\circ})$. The solid line shows the median, the darker shaded region encloses the 16th–84th percentile interval, and the lighter shaded region shows the full range of solutions. Bottom: fractional 16th–84th percentile spread in the inferred single-scattering albedo, $(\omega_{84}-\omega_{16})/\omega_{\rm median}$.

Figure 4: 
Representative multi-angular bidirectional reflectance measurements from the BUG dataset for a returned Apollo lunar soil and a Mars soil analog. The broad angular coverage samples a wide range of incidence and emergence geometries, directly constraining the phase-angle dependence of particulate surface scattering. In contrast to single-geometry laboratory spectra, such datasets provide direct information on the angular scattering behavior required to model disk-integrated reflected-light observations of rocky exoplanets.

Figure 5: Posterior distributions of the Hapke parameters for Apollo 12 soil sample 12001 at 550 nm. The left panel compares the retrieval using the restricted single-geometry subset (red) with that using the full multi-geometry BUG dataset (blue). The values above the diagonal panels indicate the median and 16th–84th percentile credible intervals for the single-geometry retrieval. The right panel shows the multi-geometry posterior on an expanded scale, with the corresponding median and 16th–84th percentile credible intervals. The much broader single-geometry posterior illustrates the strong parameter degeneracies introduced by limited angular sampling.

Figure 6: 
Comparison between the BUG multi-angular measurements and the retrieved Hapke model for the Mars analog at 550 nm. Top: measured radiance factors and predictions from the posterior-median multi-angular retrieval, evaluated at the same incidence, emergence, and phase angles as each laboratory measurement. Bottom: fractional residuals, defined as $100(r_{\rm obs}-r_{\rm model})/r_{\rm obs}$. The dashed horizontal lines indicate $\pm 10\%$ residuals. The comparison provides a direct assessment of the ability of the retrieved photometric solution to reproduce the measured angular scattering behavior.

Figure 7: 
Band-integrated phase curves for three representative wavelength regimes: reflection-dominated (0.52–0.60 $\mu$m), mixed reflection–thermal (1.55–1.75 $\mu$m), and thermal-dominated (3.8–5.0 $\mu$m). The shaded regions indicate the range of disk-integrated phase curves predicted by photometric parameter sets consistent with the same single-geometry laboratory reflectance spectrum. The darker shaded region corresponds to the central 68% interval, while the lighter region shows the full extent of the solutions. The black solid line represents the median predicted phase curve, and the red dashed line corresponds to the reference laboratory reflectance behavior. The gray dashed line shows the prediction of a simplified photometric model assuming isotropic scattering ($b=0$) and no opposition effects ($B_{0}=0$), with the single-scattering albedo adjusted to reproduce the laboratory reflectance at the reference geometry. Although this simplified model matches the laboratory measurement by construction, it produces substantial systematic biases in the predicted reflected-light observables away from the measurement geometry.

Figure 8: 
Disk-integrated reflected-light phase curves at $0.55\,\mu$m for a TRAPPIST-1$b$-like configuration using an Apollo regolith analog (sample 10084) from the BUG dataset [57]. The light-blue region shows the uncertainty envelope obtained from single-geometry laboratory conditioning. The green region corresponds to the case where additional grain-scale optical priors constrain $\omega$ and b. The red region shows the predictions obtained using the full multi-angular BUG dataset. Shaded regions represent the propagated posterior uncertainty in the Hapke parameters $(\omega,b,B_{0},h)$. The vertical gray band marks the approximate phase-angle range corresponding to secondary-eclipse ingress. Although grain-scale optical constraints partially reduce the uncertainty envelope, substantial uncertainty remains until direct multi-angular constraints are introduced.

Figure 9: 
Disk-integrated reflected-light phase curves obtained under simplified photometric assumptions for the TRAPPIST-1b example considered in this work. The blue shaded region shows the uncertainty envelope obtained when the phase-function asymmetry parameter is fixed ($b=0$) while retaining the full photometric model. The red shaded region corresponds to the case where opposition effects are neglected during the inversion stage, allowing the single-scattering albedo to be uniquely inferred at the laboratory geometry and then propagated using the full model. In both cases, the solutions reproduce the same laboratory reflectance at the reference geometry but retain broad uncertainty when extrapolated to other phase angles. The two approximations produce broadly similar phase-curve morphologies, with the largest uncertainty occurring toward small phase angles where opposition effects strongly influence the reflected signal.

Figure 10: 
Posterior distributions of the geometric albedo $A_{g}$ predicted under the three conditioning schemes considered in this work. The violin distributions show the posterior geometric albedo $A_{g}$ for the single-geometry retrieval (left), the single-geometry retrieval supplemented by grain-scale optical constraints (center), and the full multi-angular retrieval (right). Black points and vertical bars indicate the posterior medians and 16th–84th percentile intervals, respectively. The individual posterior samples are shown as faint black points.

2610.28755.abstract: The first observations of short-period rocky exoplanets have initiated the era of terrestrial exoplanet characterization. The interpretation of these observations relies on forward models used in atmospheric and surface retrieval frameworks. While atmospheric modeling is supported by extensive laboratory datasets of molecular opacities, the experimental basis for rocky surface characterization remains limited. Most reflectance libraries of planetary analog materials provide spectra measured at a single illumination and viewing geometry, constraining the spectral behavior but not its full angular scattering properties. We show that incomplete angular coverage in laboratory bidirectional reflectance measurements introduces an intrinsic systematic uncertainty in the interpretation of rocky exoplanet observations. We demonstrate that multiple combinations of photometric parameters can reproduce the same laboratory reflectance spectrum while predicting different angular scattering behaviors and disk-integrated observables. We propagate this non-uniqueness to reflected-light phase curves, geometric albedos, and planet-star contrast ratios between $0.5$--$1.7\,\mu$m, representative of the spectral range targeted by future direct-imaging missions such as the HWO. We find that single-geometry laboratory spectra produce large uncertainties in predicted signals, particularly at small phase angles. Simplified assumptions adopted in exoplanet studies, such as isotropic scattering can additionally introduce systematic biases. Using multi-angular laboratory measurements from the Bloomsburg University Goniometer dataset, we show that the uncertainty in predicted observables collapses once angular scattering behavior is directly constrained. Our results demonstrate that multi-angular measurements are required to construct physically predictive reflected-light models of rocky exoplanets.

2610.28795.abstract: Recent molecular line observations with high spatial resolutions have revealed vertical chemical stratification in Class I/II disks (i.e. chemical composition changing with height in the vertical direction of the disk), as well as a radial variation of ionisation rates. However, such chemical layered structures in Class 0 disk and envelope systems have been investigated only for limited objects, such as L1527. In the context of the ALMA Large Program FAUST, we report the results of molecular line observations toward the disk and envelope around the low-mass Class 0 protostar NGC 1333 IRAS 4C in the Perseus Molecular Cloud. Previous observations have shown that the disk rotation axis of this object is largely tilted to the line of sight, making it suitable for studying the molecular abundance distribution as a function of disk height. We found that the molecules known as gas density tracers such as C18O and H2CO are distributed around the disk midplane. In addition, molecules known as tracers of photochemical reactions such as CCH and c-C3H2 are distributed in the low-density upper layers of the disk, unlike the distribution in L1527. Moreover, the column density ratio of HCO+/CO derived from the H13CO+ and C18O line emission suggests that the ionisation degree and the ionisation rate vary with the disk radius and they are larger in the outer region of the disk and envelope.

2610.28896.abstract: Context. Atmospheric pollution in white dwarfs is interpreted as evidence for the accretion of rocky material from remnant planetary systems. Wide binary companions can influence the delivery of planetary material onto white dwarfs, making it essential to understand the interplay between stellar evolution and binary perturbations. Aims. We investigate how uncertainties in stellar mass-loss histories affect the dynamical evolution of remnant planetary systems in wide binaries, and assess their relative importance compared with binary perturbations in driving the accretion of rocky material onto white dwarfs. Methods. We perform REBOUND N-body simulations incorporating time-dependent stellar parameters interpolated from MESA evolutionary tracks and tidal interactions, following the dynamical evolution up to the white dwarf stage. We explore two stellar-evolution models with distinct mass-loss histories for wide binary systems hosting a Jupiter-mass planet and a planetesimal disc, spanning a range of binary architectures. Results. The adopted stellar-evolution model has only a minor effect on the survival of the planet, mainly affecting the timing and efficiency of planetesimal delivery during the white dwarf stage. Instead, the architecture of the binary primarily controls the pollution outcome: wider binaries produce the highest rates of accretion onto the white dwarf, consistent with the observed prevalence of polluted white dwarfs in wide binaries. Moreover, planetesimal reservoirs remain long-lived, with survival times increasing with binary separation, enabling Gyr-long metal pollution. Conclusions. Our results suggest that the architecture of wide binaries, rather than uncertainties in stellar evolution, is the dominant factor controlling the dynamical delivery of rocky material onto white dwarfs.

2610.29383.title: Surface regolith model of near-Earth asteroid (3200) Phaethon

figures.caption:
Figure 1: Flowchart of the simulation process.
Small particles are first calculated using absMie for olivine and troilite, from which multi-particle media are created that are used as surface roughness and internal inclusions in large olivine-hosted particles. The large olivine-hosted particles are simulated using SIRIS4 and the troilite aggregate particles using ADDA. A regolith medium is created from the two large particle species. Observables are finally calculated of the regolith medium using SIRIS4 and RT-CB.

Figure 2: Predicted reflectance spectra of the best-fit model compared to observed spectra. The MITHNEOS 2024 spectrum of Phaethon was used as the comparison against which the model was constructed, as it is a recent spectral observation with a large wavelength coverage and a dense wavelength sampling. The model is accurately able to produce the spectrum in the whole Vis-NIR wavelength range.

Figure 5: Comparison of Vis-spectral results from the original model with troilite aggregate size distribution exponent of $u_{\text{T1}}=5.3$ and $u_{\text{T1}}=5.5$. The smaller exponent value of the weight function accurately models the bluer spectra (Spectrum 16-1 and 16-2) from Lazzarin et al. [38], and physically translates to a larger abundance of smaller troilite particles between the regoliths. All other spectral slopes that can be found between the two simulation results could also be modeled by changing the exponent value.

Figure 6: Polarization result for a model where the packing density of troilite aggregate particles has been halved from 0.02% of the original model to 0.01%. By halving the amount of troilite aggregates, a good fit to the higher polarization observations of Ito et al. [26] is achieved.

2610.29383.abstract: The near-Earth asteroid (3200) Phaethon displays activity as it comes close to the Sun and is presumed to be the progenitor of the Geminids meteor shower. Both CM- and CY-meteorites have been suggested as possible meteorite analogues for Phaethon. Previous spectral and polarization measurements of Phaethon indicate possible surface heterogeneity in the regolith properties. By combining mineral components and their size fractions, we present a regolith model for Phaethon that reproduces the spectral, polarization, and geometric albedo measurements presented in various studies, with the aim of quantitatively characterizing the surface material and structure, as well as the regolith heterogeneity. The best fit model able to produce the measurements is constructed from large olivine particles with troilite inclusions and small scale surface roughness, mixed with smaller, porous troilite aggregates comprised of monomers resembling interplanetary dust. Our model suggests that the different spectral and polarization responses of the regolith are caused by changes in the size and amount of the small dark troilite particles. Based on the amount of troilite in the regolith model, we propose that CM-meteorites are the preferable meteorite analogue for Phaethon.

2610.29459.abstract: V1298 Tau is a very young and magnetically active K1V star which hosts a benchmark multi-planetary system to study planet formation and evolutionary history at the earliest stages. Between 2025 and 2026, we conducted a campaign to monitor the variability of V1298 Tau in radio (band C), X-ray, and NUV bands, with the support of publicly available contemporary optical light curve, and to investigate multi-band correlations to link the emission with stellar activity. Radio observations were carried out with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) in band C (4.5--6.5 GHz). X-ray and NUV observations were carried out with the Swift satellite over 20 days, ending one month before the begin of the radio campaign. We analysed the temporal variability of peak (integrated) fluxes in the C-band and of X-ray (NUV) luminosities on various timescales, comparing it with the variability observed in the high-cadence optical light curve collected by the ASAS-SN survey. We observed both radio and high-energy time variable emission. JVLA detected emission in 90\% of the visits, switching between high ($\geq$0.1 mJy/beam) and low flux states in matter of days or hours. The fluxes show moderate correlation with the optical light curve, suggesting modulation with the stellar rotation period. Except for one visit, dynamic spectral analysis does not reveal short-term (minutes) variability, nor is there any evidence of circularly polarised emissions. Overall, the radio observations can be explained as gyrosynchrotron and/or cyclotron emission from the corona, and linked to stellar magnetic activity. At high-energy, we detected significant variability in X-ray luminosity (within the range ~1.2--2.5x10$^{+30}$ erg/s), the decay phase of a stellar flare, and evidence of correlation with the optical flux. Our data confirm that V1298\,Tau follows the near-linear Güdel-Benz relation.

2610.29610.abstract: We report the discovery and characterization of a planetary system in the microlensing event OGLE-2013-BLG-1125/MOA-2013-BLG-584. We analyze photometric data from OGLE and MOA surveys, as well as LCO, $\mu$FUN, and Mindstep follow-up telescopes to model the microlensing light curve. We also used data from the Keck II telescope collected in 2018 to obtain additional constraints on the lensing system. We found a Saturn-mass planet of mass $M_{\rm p}=105\pm13 \ M_\oplus$ orbiting a low-mass host star $M_{\rm L}=0.139\pm0.011 \ M_\odot$ at $1.00\pm0.08$ kpc from Earth. This discovery adds to the small sample of giant planets orbiting low-mass stars and provides constraints on planet formation theories.

2610.29805.abstract: Contact binaries, appearing as two objects stuck together, are prevalent throughout the Solar System, making up between 30- 50% of asteroids and comets. Despite this, detailed shape models of contact binaries are hard to obtain remotely, requiring rare occultation events or close approaches to Earth (< 0.1 au) to observe with ground-based radar systems. Despite only 16 contact binary models being published, there already exists a wide variety of different arrangements of the two lobes relative to one another. At the same time, simulations of contact binary object formation are increasing in scale, producing 10s to 1000s of contact binary candidates per simulation. It is therefore necessary to begin the process of characterising the different shapes observed, and to further investigate any emerging trends. We analyse the size, period, neck prominence, volume distribution, ratio between the sizes and volumes of the individual lobes, and the alignment between them to summarise the extent of the currently modelled asteroids.

2610.29930.abstract: Titan's equatorial superrotation is associated with climatological retrograde (westward) near-surface winds at low latitudes, as consistently simulated by Titan general circulation models. However, the Huygens probe measured prograde (eastward) near-surface winds, contrary to the expected circulation. We investigate whether these observations reflect localized forcing by large-scale topography, using paired three-dimensional dry simulations with and without topography in the Titan Atmospheric Model. We find that topography generates longitude-locked, vertically structured zonal wind anomalies that reproduce key features of the Huygens wind profile in the lowest few kilometers. Helmholtz and spectral analyses show that this structure arises from the superposition of several vertically varying low wavenumber modes. A predominantly rotational, topographically forced stationary zonal wavenumber s=1 response provides a major eastward anomaly throughout the lowest 2 km, whereas a locally divergent s=4 response consistent with a gravity wave, opposes it near the surface. Weaker s=2 and s=3 responses also vary vertically and contribute eastward anomalies near the surface. Combined with the retrograde zonal-mean circulation, these modes produce a Huygens-like profile characterized by prograde flow within the lowest 1 km and shear toward retrograde flow aloft. The paired simulations establish their topographic origin, while coherence with the corresponding terrain-forcing components demonstrates that the responses remain phase locked to the forcing. Similar but weaker stationary responses are simulated near the planned Dragonfly landing site, providing baseline expectations for interpreting its future atmospheric measurements. This study demonstrates how large-scale topography can generate localized departures from Titan's zonal-mean circulation and highlights the importance of stationary waves.

2610.30115.title: Predictions for an unseen third planet in the WISPIT 2 system

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic edge-on view of the inner part of the WISPIT 2 system. Dotted and dashed lines indicate the positions of the peaks of the rings detected using VLT/SPHERE and ALMA, respectively. The solid grey region marks the location of faint millimetre dust detected by van der Marel et al. [53]. The ALMA ring at 144.4 au sits unusually far from the outermost planet, WISPIT 2b, so may hint at the presence of a third planet between $\sim$100–140 au.

Figure 2: Mass–SMA parameter space for a potential, unseen planet in WISPIT 2. The solid dark grey line marks the range of possible masses and semi-major axes for the planet according to Faruqi et al. [17, equation 11], with errors denoted by the surrounding shaded region. The dotted and dashed lines mark the central locations of the observed SPHERE and ALMA rings, respectively. The dark grey dot-dashed line indicates the predicted location of a ring produced by WISPIT 2b, which agrees with the observed SPHERE ring. The hatched regions indicate the “forbidden zones” i.e., the regions of the parameter space we do not predict a planet can exist due to observational constraints (the SPHERE and MagAO-X H$\alpha$ detection ranges), the presence of rings, or the limit due to the gap-opening timescale exceeding the 5.1 Myr age of the system.

Figure 3: Zoomed in version of Figure 2 but with the Kanagawa et al. [30], Kanagawa et al. [31] gap and depth prescriptions overlaid. Since the depth of the gas gap has not been directly measured, we plot the depth relation for a number of different values of $\Sigma_{p}/\Sigma_{0}$ and find that all three prescriptions intersect at a depth of 0.2.

2610.30115.abstract: We predict the mass and semi-major axis of a currently unseen but hypothesised planet in the WISPIT 2 system based on the location of the ring observed by ALMA at 144.4 au. Using findings from previous hydrodynamical models, we predict that a ~0.2-1 $M_{Jup}$ planet may exist at ~ 100-120 au. We also demonstrate that the ring seen in VLT/SPHERE observations at 96.7 au is consistent with the mass and semi-major axis of WISPIT 2b and confirm that WISPIT 2b cannot be the cause of the ALMA ring. We also discuss how future observations of the system's gas component may help constrain these predictions better, and note that this third planet in WISPIT 2 may be discoverable using upcoming JWST/NIRCam observations or Gaia data release 4 (DR4).

2610.28687.title: Solar System Surface Technosignatures: Searching for Signs of Artificial Design on Extraterrestrial Terrain

figures.caption: Figure 1: Three examples of surface technosignatures on Earth that are over 500 years old and are visible in orbital satellite imagery: 1) Ziggurat of Ur 2) Inca Agricultural Terraces and 3) Pyramid of the Sun. The a) images show the structures from a near-surface perspective while the b) images are representative of the structures appearance in satellite imagery, as sourced from Google Maps. Two takeaways can be drawn here: surface technosignatures can be readily identified from satellite imagery, and we have a large, consistent training dataset of examples of human surface technosignatures from the Earth itself. Image credits: © Ziggurat of Ur: Qahtan Al-Abeed — © Inca Agricultural Terraces: PsamatheM — © Pyramid of the Sun: Burkhard Mücke

2610.28687.abstract: Artificial radio emissions have historically been a major focus of technosignature searches. Here, we apply an anthropological lens to expand this scope to surface technosignatures: non-random, intentional patterning on planetary terrain, similar to long-lasting human-made landscapes and monuments on Earth. On geologically inactive bodies such as the Moon and Mars, artificial traces and patterns could potentially remain visible for hundreds of millions of years. We discuss two recent developments that make this search timely: high-resolution imaging datasets, such as those produced by the HiRISE camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and ML-based anomaly-detection methods. Finally, we list two possible approaches to developing a model capable of searching for these surface technosignatures: a supervised and an unsupervised one. Complemented by LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar, and reflectance spectroscopy, these methods would enable the first quantitative upper limits on surface technosignatures while yielding ancillary benefits for planetary science.

2610.30028.title: The Pandora SmallSat: Target Selection and Early Science

figures.caption: Figure 1: A summary of the Pandora mission’s capabilities and goals. Pandora can uniquely perform simultaneous visible photometry and near infrared spectroscopy of individual targets on a space-based platform. In a sun-synchronous, low Earth orbit (LEO), Pandora has the ability to dwell on targets for long (days-weeks) periods of time, enabling us to probe stellar contamination over the rotation periods of Pandora’s target stars.

Figure 2: In order to select our final Prime Mission targets, we plotted each target in our long list to show the range of planet radius and stellar host effective temperatures covered. We selected the top 10 gaseous (above 1.9 R⊕) and top 10 terrestrial (below 1.9 R⊕) targets to be our 20 Prime Mission targets, as indicated by the black ringed points. An additional 20 targets were selected as Secondary Targets as backups to the Prime Mission targets, shown with red rings.

Figure 3: An example of our spectral overlap analysis for GJ 3090. Left: A simulate starfield with synthetic Pandora spectral traces in realistic brightnesses and orientations for the star field. The size of Pandora’s NIRDA detector is denoted by the light blue box. Right: A representation of the spectral overlap when the star field is rotated to every possible orientation. Colors represent amount of total flux at different wavelengths in the trace compared to the amount of flux from the target trace.

2610.30028.abstract: The Pandora spacecraft is a smallsat selected in NASA's inaugural class of Pioneers missions. The aim of the Pandora mission is to disentangle stellar activity signals from exoplanet atmospheric transmission spectroscopy measurements. Pandora accomplishes this goal with its combined visible photometry and NIR spectroscopy that observe each target in the prime mission for 10 separate transit observations, each spanning 24 hours at a time. Targets were carefully selected for the Pandora prime mission. Pandora is specifically studying planets around low-mass stellar hosts (K and M dwarf stars) spanning a range of rotation periods and activity levels. The planets range in size from 1.5 - 15 Earth radii and orbital periods ranging from 1.7 - 11.5 days. In addition to the 10 transit visits planned for each of the 20 prime mission targets, Pandora is observing a number of auxiliary targets encompassing a variety of science topics. This includes topics such as stellar activity and young systems, transit timing variations of exoplanets, brown dwarf compositions, exoplanet phase curves, etc. We will discuss the selection of these targets, how they have been scheduled to fill in gaps in prime mission operations, and early science results. If the mission is extended, there is further opportunity for accomplishing additional science. Here we will discuss the possible options for extended mission operations and science.
